rationale: A wins because it does the thing founders hate and journalists require: it separates pitchable news from missing proof without sanding off the hard questions. Its strongest angle, “Wise will roll out stablecoin settlement one regulator at a time,” turns the regulatory rollout into a real beat story and then admits the stablecoin name and first markets are mandatory. B is good, but “Stablecoins get a mainstream payments test” leans toward category wallpaper, and “SWIFT-rail economics” drags in a term the update did not give it. A has sharper lanes, cleaner proof gates, and the useful second-wave customer angle B throws away too early.
gaps_in_A: “A listed, profitable payments company is now settling business transfers in stablecoin” is close to overclaiming mainstream/category significance; A saves it with proof requirements, but the headline still needs the unnamed stablecoin and actual markets before it deserves oxygen.
“The first-market decision is the news that keeps the story open” assumes a first market is available; the update says region-by-region, not that Wise named a launch market.
“Investor” angle needs more than “publicly listed and profitable”; without unit-cost or volume guidance, it may collapse into an analyst question rather than a story.
gaps_in_B: “Stablecoins get a mainstream payments test” is a mushier category frame than it looks; one Wise launch is a data point, not a trend, unless B brings comparable regulated payments moves.
“SWIFT-rail economics” is sloppy shorthand and partly invented from “correspondent-banking system”; SWIFT is not the same thing as settlement economics, and a banking reporter will notice.
“Which bank fees and float revenue get squeezed” is plausible but not grounded tightly enough in the update; it turns a cost claim into a bank-revenue claim without proof.
“How one business cut its settlement costs…” is refused as hallucinated, but B misses the more useful version: a second-wave customer story once a named business, corridor, amount, and savings exist.
